analogy.p: Think of each molecule as a tight, unbreakable knot of paper clips (the strong covalent bonds), and the molecules as being held to one another only by weak sticky tape. To separate the knots you just peel off the tape, which is easy, so the knots themselves stay intact (low melting and boiling points). A polymer is like a bowl of long spaghetti: each strand is strong (covalent bonds along the chain), but because each strand is so long it touches its neighbours in thousands of places, so a lot of sticky tape holds the bowl together, and the whole lump is solid. It breaks down because real intermolecular forces are not glue and arise from attractions between charges in neighbouring molecules.
analogy.t: Strong chains in a bowl of spaghetti and sticky notes

bullets: Covalent bonding occurs between **non-metals** (for example H, C, N, O, Cl); it does not form a lattice of ions.
Each shared pair of electrons = **one single covalent bond**; two shared pairs make a **double bond** (O=O, C=O); three make a **triple bond** (N≡N).
Most non-metal atoms share electrons until they have a **full outer shell** (hydrogen needs 2, the others need 8).
Examples of simple molecular substances: hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, chlorine, water, hydrogen chloride, ammonia, methane, carbon dioxide, iodine.
The covalent bonds **within** a molecule are strong; the **intermolecular forces** between molecules are weak. This difference explains all the properties.
Covalent molecules can be elements (H2, O2, Cl2) or compounds (H2O, CO2).
Do not confuse small molecules with **giant covalent** structures (diamond, silicon dioxide), where covalent bonds join millions of atoms into a lattice.
core.h: Covalent bonding and what a small molecule is
core.p: A **covalent bond** is a **shared pair of electrons** between two atoms. It forms between **non-metal atoms**, which each need to gain electrons to fill their outer shell, so instead of transferring electrons they **share** them. Each shared pair is attracted to the nuclei of both atoms, which holds the atoms together, so covalent bonds are **strong**. Atoms joined by covalent bonds form **molecules**. A **small molecule** (simple molecular substance) contains only a **few atoms**, for example hydrogen H2, water H2O, carbon dioxide CO2, methane CH4 and ammonia NH3. The key idea for this topic is that the **atoms inside a molecule are held by strong covalent bonds, but the molecules themselves are only held to each other by weak forces**.

bullets: **Dot and cross**: shows which atom each electron comes from and the lone pairs; does **not** show the shape of the molecule or relative size.
**Displayed formula**: shows every atom and each bond as a line (H–Cl, O=O); does **not** show the shape accurately or the electrons.
**Ball and stick**: shows the 3D arrangement and bond angles; the sticks make it look as if the bonds are physical rods, and it does not show electrons or the relative sizes accurately.
**2D diagrams** (drawn on paper) cannot show 3D shape, so methane drawn flat is a limitation.
A **lone pair** (non-bonding pair) is a pair of outer electrons that is not shared with another atom; water has two lone pairs on oxygen.
Exam tip: when asked for a limitation, name the model and say what it **does not show**.
Link: these ideas are used again to draw alkanes and polymers in the organic chemistry topics.
core.h: Representing covalent molecules: dot and cross, displayed and 3D models
core.p: You need to be able to **draw and interpret** several ways of representing covalent molecules. A **dot and cross diagram** shows only the **outer-shell electrons**, with electrons from one atom as dots and from the other as crosses, and a shared pair sits where the two outer shells **overlap**. A **displayed formula** uses one line for each shared pair, so it shows how atoms are joined but not electrons. **Ball and stick models** and **3D models** show the shape of the molecule and the angles between bonds. Each model has strengths and limitations, and you should be able to say what each model does and does not show.

bullets: **H2**: two H atoms share **one pair** (each H then has 2 electrons, a full first shell).
**Cl2**: each Cl has 7 outer electrons and shares **one pair**, giving 8 each; each Cl keeps three lone pairs.
**O2**: each O has 6 outer electrons and they share **two pairs** (a double bond), giving 8 each.
**N2**: each N has 5 outer electrons and they share **three pairs** (a triple bond), giving 8 each.
**HCl**: H and Cl share one pair; Cl has 8 outer electrons including three lone pairs.
**H2O**: O shares one pair with each of two H atoms, leaving **two lone pairs** on oxygen (8 outer electrons).
**NH3**: N shares one pair with each of three H atoms, leaving **one lone pair**.
**CH4**: C shares one pair with each of four H atoms, leaving no lone pairs; **CO2**: C shares **two pairs** with each O (two double bonds).
Check: add up the electrons around each atom; hydrogen should have 2, every other atom 8.
core.h: Drawing dot and cross diagrams step by step
core.p: To draw a dot and cross diagram, first work out how many electrons each atom needs to complete its outer shell. Then draw the outer shells overlapping and place **shared pairs** in the overlaps. Count to check that every atom ends up with a **full outer shell**. Practise with hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen chloride, water, ammonia, methane and carbon dioxide, because these are the examples that appear most often. In the diagram below, each shared pair has one dot and one cross, and the two non-bonding pairs on oxygen are the lone pairs.

bullets: **Intermolecular** means *between* molecules; **intramolecular** (covalent) means *within* molecules.
Intermolecular forces are much weaker than covalent bonds, so little energy is needed to overcome them.
The covalent bonds stay unbroken during melting and boiling: when water boils it is still H2O molecules in the gas, not hydrogen and oxygen.
Intermolecular forces also hold the molecules in a **regular pattern in solids** such as iodine and solid carbon dioxide.
The forces get **stronger as molecules get bigger** (more electrons and larger relative formula mass).
At GCSE you only need the idea of 'weak intermolecular forces'; names for different types of intermolecular forces are not needed.
Because the forces are weak, small molecular substances are often soft solids when they are solid (for example iodine crystals, wax).
core.h: Intermolecular forces: the weak forces between molecules
core.p: **Intermolecular forces** are the forces of attraction **between molecules**. They are **weak compared with covalent bonds**, which is why molecules stay intact while the forces between them can be overcome easily. They are not covalent bonds and they are not 'bonds between atoms'. When a simple molecular substance melts or boils, it is the **weak intermolecular forces** that are overcome, **not the strong covalent bonds** inside the molecules. This is the single most important idea in this topic: if you remember that the covalent bonds do **not** break, you will avoid the most common mistake in exam answers.

bullets: Weak intermolecular forces → **little energy** to overcome → **low** melting and boiling points.
Examples: oxygen boils at about −183 °C, nitrogen at about −196 °C and methane at about −162 °C, so they are gases at room temperature.
Bromine is a liquid at room temperature (melts at about −7 °C, boils at about 59 °C) and iodine is a solid (melts at about 114 °C).
Do **not** say 'the covalent bonds are weak': the covalent bonds are strong; the **intermolecular forces** are weak.
Particle ideas: as a solid melts, molecules gain energy and move; in a gas the molecules are far apart and the forces between them are negligible.
Link: states of matter, particle model and energy changes.
core.h: Why small molecular substances have low melting and boiling points
core.p: Small molecules have **low melting points and boiling points** because only a **small amount of energy** is needed to overcome the **weak intermolecular forces**. The molecules are separated from each other while the strong covalent bonds inside them stay intact. As a result, many simple molecular substances are **gases or liquids at room temperature**, and the solids that exist (such as iodine) melt easily. A good exam answer says: 'the intermolecular forces are weak so little energy is needed to overcome them'. It never says the covalent bonds break.

bullets: Halogens boiling points (rounded): F2 about −188 °C, Cl2 about −34 °C, Br2 about 59 °C, I2 about 184 °C; relative formula masses 38, 71, 160 and 254.
Alkanes boiling points (rounded): methane −162 °C, ethane −89 °C, propane −42 °C, butane about −1 °C, pentane 36 °C, hexane 69 °C.
Describe the trend using numbers: 'as Mr increases from 71 to 160, the boiling point rises from −34 °C to 59 °C'.
Explain the trend: bigger molecules → stronger intermolecular forces → more energy needed → higher boiling point.
For graphs of boiling point against Mr, expect an upward curve rather than a straight line; the pattern is 'as one increases, so does the other'.
Higher-tier thinking: a longer chain has more points of contact with neighbouring chains, so the total force is greater.
Do not say 'the bonds are stronger' for bigger molecules: it is the **intermolecular forces** that increase.
core.h: How the size of the molecule affects melting and boiling point
core.p: The **larger the molecule**, the **stronger the intermolecular forces**, so **more energy** is needed to overcome them and the melting point and boiling point **increase** with relative formula mass. Larger molecules have more electrons and more contact with neighbouring molecules, so the total attraction between them is greater. This explains the trend in the halogens: fluorine and chlorine are gases at room temperature, bromine is a liquid, and iodine is a solid. It also explains the trend in the alkanes: methane is a gas but longer-chain alkanes are liquids and then waxy solids.

bullets: Molecules are **neutral**: equal numbers of protons and electrons, so there are no charged particles to move.
All outer electrons are held in covalent bonds or lone pairs and cannot move between molecules.
Water (pure) and liquid hydrocarbons (for example petrol) are non-conductors.

Extension: some molecular compounds react with water to form ions (for example hydrogen chloride forms hydrogen ions and chloride ions in water, so the solution conducts), but the **pure molecular substance** does not.
In exam answers use the phrase 'no overall electric charge' or 'no free ions or electrons'.
Link: compare with the properties of ionic compounds and metals.
core.h: Why small molecules do not conduct electricity
core.p: Substances conduct electricity if they contain **charged particles that are free to move**: free electrons in metals, or ions in molten or dissolved ionic compounds. Small molecules have **no overall electric charge** and **no free electrons or ions**, since all the electrons are in the covalent bonds or lone pairs of the molecule. So simple molecular substances **do not conduct electricity** in any state, solid, liquid or gas. This is a key way to tell them apart from ionic compounds (which conduct when molten) and metals (which conduct when solid).

bullets: **Polymer** = a substance made up of very large molecules, formed from many small monomer molecules joined together.
Atoms in the chain are joined by **strong covalent bonds**; intermolecular forces between the chains are **relatively strong** compared with those between small molecules.
Poly(ethene) is made from ethene monomers (C2H4); poly(propene) is made from propene.
Because polymers are very large, they have high relative formula masses (often tens of thousands).
Polymers are **solids at room temperature**, unlike ethene, which is a gas.
Most polymers do not conduct electricity (no charged particles free to move).
Link: addition polymerisation and alkenes in the organic chemistry unit.
core.p: **Polymers** are substances made of **very large molecules**. The atoms in the polymer molecules are linked to other atoms by **strong covalent bonds**, forming long chains (often thousands of atoms long). Polymers form when many small molecules called **monomers** join together by **addition polymerisation**; for example many ethene molecules join to make **poly(ethene)**. The **intermolecular forces** between polymer molecules are **relatively strong**, because the molecules are so large, and so these substances are **solids at room temperature**. The covalent bonds within each chain are the same strong bonds as in small molecules; what is different is that the molecules are huge.

bullets: Small molecule: few contacts between molecules → weak total force → gas or liquid.
Polymer: long chains lie alongside each other with many contacts → strong total force → solid.
Longer chains mean stronger intermolecular forces, and so a higher melting temperature.
Covalent bonds are not broken when polymers soften or melt, only intermolecular forces (though heating too much can decompose a polymer).
Model answer phrase: 'polymers are very large molecules so the intermolecular forces are relatively strong'.
core.h: Why polymers are solids at room temperature
core.p: The size of the intermolecular forces depends on the **size of the molecules**. Polymer molecules are **much larger** than small molecules, so there are many more points where one molecule is attracted to its neighbours, and the **total** intermolecular attraction is much greater. A lot more energy is needed to separate the chains, so polymers are **solids at room temperature**. This is the same reasoning as the trend in alkanes and halogens, taken to extremes: the bigger the molecule, the stronger the intermolecular forces. Small molecules like ethene (Mr 28) are gases, but poly(ethene) with chains of thousands of repeat units is a solid.

bullets: The **repeating unit** is the smallest section that repeats along the chain; it is shown inside brackets with the bonds continuing through the brackets.
Poly(ethene): –(CH2–CH2)n–; each carbon has four bonds (two to H and two along the chain).
Mr of polymer = Mr of repeating unit × n.
The number of repeat units n = Mr of polymer ÷ Mr of repeat unit.
In displayed form, the chain continues with dashes (single bonds) at both ends of the brackets.
From a diagram of part of a chain, identify the repeat unit by finding the group of atoms that repeats.
core.p: A polymer molecule is a long chain made of the same **repeating unit** over and over. We show the polymer by drawing the **repeating unit** in brackets with the letter **n** after it, where n is a very large number. For poly(ethene), the repeating unit is –CH2–CH2– and the polymer is written as –(CH2–CH2)n–. The relative formula mass of the polymer equals the relative formula mass of the repeating unit multiplied by n. For example, the repeating unit of poly(ethene) has Mr = 12 × 2 + 1 × 4 = 28, so a chain with 1000 repeat units has Mr = 28 000.

bullets: Low mp, no conduction → **small molecule**.
Solid at room temperature but soft or flexible, no conduction → likely **polymer**.
Very high mp, no conduction → **giant covalent** (diamond, silicon dioxide).
High mp, conducts only when molten/dissolved → **ionic**.
Conducts when solid → **metal** (or graphite).
What gets overcome when it melts: small molecule – intermolecular forces; ionic – electrostatic forces between ions; giant covalent – covalent bonds; metal – metallic bonds.
core.h: Comparing small molecules, polymers, giant covalent and ionic substances
core.p: Many exam questions ask you to decide what type of structure a substance has from its properties. **Small molecules** have low melting and boiling points, are gases, liquids or soft solids, and never conduct. **Polymers** are solids with higher melting temperatures than small molecules because of their larger intermolecular forces, and do not conduct. **Giant covalent** substances have very high melting points because strong covalent bonds must be broken. **Ionic** compounds have high melting points and conduct when molten or dissolved. **Metals** conduct when solid. Use melting point, state and conductivity to identify.

bullets: State at 20 °C: below the melting point = solid; between melting and boiling = liquid; above the boiling point = gas.
Example: chlorine mp −101 °C, bp −34 °C → gas at 20 °C; bromine mp −7 °C, bp 59 °C → liquid; iodine mp 114 °C → solid.
Describe: 'as the relative formula mass increases, the boiling point increases'; then explain with intermolecular forces.
A graph of boiling point against Mr usually slopes up; read values from the axes carefully, including negative temperatures.
Be careful with the word 'bond': for melting of small molecules write 'intermolecular forces'.
core.h: Using data: identifying the substance and describing trends
core.p: You will be given tables of melting points, boiling points and conductivity and be asked to identify the type of structure or describe a trend. Read the units and the temperature carefully, and compare the melting and boiling point to **room temperature (about 20 °C)** to work out the state. A substance is a **gas** if its boiling point is below room temperature, a **liquid** if its melting point is below and boiling point is above room temperature, and a **solid** if its melting point is above room temperature. Quote numbers when describing a trend.

bullets: Fractional distillation of crude oil separates hydrocarbons by boiling point, which depends on molecule size.
The alkanes are small molecules, so they do not conduct electricity and have low boiling points.
Addition polymerisation: many ethene molecules join to make poly(ethene).
Compare ionic and covalent bonding when asked about the type of bonding in a substance.
Atoms in a molecule are joined by covalent bonds; molecules are held to each other by intermolecular forces.
Always check whether the question refers to what is **between** molecules or **within** molecules.
core.h: Common misconceptions and links to other topics
core.p: The most common error is to say that the **covalent bonds break** when a small molecular substance melts or boils. They do not: it is only the weak intermolecular forces. A second common error is to say that covalent bonds are weak because the substance has a low melting point; the covalent bonds are strong. This topic links to **states of matter** (energy changes and particle models), to **organic chemistry** (alkanes, alkenes, addition polymerisation, trends in boiling point), to **separation techniques** (fractional distillation uses differences in boiling point caused by molecule size) and to **bonding** (comparing with ionic and metallic).

exam: **Melting/boiling of small molecules (2 to 3 marks):** (1) intermolecular forces are weak, (2) little energy is needed to overcome them, (3) covalent bonds do not break.
**Size trend (3 to 4 marks):** larger molecules → stronger intermolecular forces → more energy needed → higher boiling point; quote Mr and temperature values.
**Conductivity (1 to 2 marks):** 'no overall electric charge' or 'no free ions or electrons'; molecules are neutral.
**Polymer solid (2 marks):** very large molecules, so the intermolecular forces are relatively strong.
**Dot and cross (2 to 3 marks):** correct shared pairs, correct lone pairs, every atom with a full outer shell.
**Displayed formula (1 to 2 marks):** a line for every bond; double bonds as two lines; check each atom has the right number of bonds (H 1, O 2, N 3, C 4).
**Evaluate a model (2 to 3 marks):** name the model, state what it shows, state what it does not show.
**Identify structure from data (2 to 4 marks):** quote melting point and conduction, name the structure type, then explain with the forces involved.
**Calculations (2 to 3 marks):** Mr of repeat unit, then Mr of polymer = Mr × n, or n = Mr of polymer ÷ Mr of repeat unit; show working and give units if needed.
**6 mark questions:** structure the answer: bonding in molecules, forces between molecules, effect of size, link to melting points and states; use the terms intermolecular and covalent correctly.
**Graph questions:** read values accurately, including negative values, and describe the shape before explaining.

mistakes.r: Only the weak intermolecular forces are overcome; the covalent bonds do not break.
mistakes.w: When a molecular substance boils the covalent bonds break.

mistakes.r: Covalent bonds are strong; the intermolecular forces between molecules are weak.
mistakes.w: Small molecules have low melting points because covalent bonds are weak.

mistakes.r: Bigger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces so more energy is needed to overcome them.
mistakes.w: Bigger molecules have stronger covalent bonds so higher boiling point.

mistakes.r: They have no overall charge and no free ions or electrons (all electrons are in bonds or lone pairs).
mistakes.w: Small molecules do not conduct because they have no electrons.

mistakes.r: Intermolecular forces act between molecules; bonds between atoms are covalent bonds.
mistakes.w: Intermolecular forces are the bonds between atoms.

mistakes.r: Polymers are solids because the molecules are large so the intermolecular forces are relatively strong.
mistakes.w: Polymers are solids because they have strong covalent bonds.

mistakes.r: Check every atom has a full outer shell; show lone pairs.
mistakes.w: Drawing a dot and cross diagram with a missing lone pair or with the wrong number of shared pairs.

mistakes.r: The repeat unit is shown in brackets with the continuation bonds through the brackets and n outside.
mistakes.w: A polymer chain is written without the n, or the brackets are closed.

mistakes.r: Boiling water gives water vapour (H2O molecules): the covalent bonds stay intact.
mistakes.w: Water boils to give hydrogen and oxygen.

summary: The specification asks you to describe small molecules as having strong covalent bonds within molecules but weak intermolecular forces between them, so they have low melting and boiling points, get higher with molecular size, and do not conduct electricity; and to describe polymers as very large molecules with strong covalent bonds and relatively strong intermolecular forces, so they are solids at room temperature. It matters because the idea that melting only overcomes intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds, is tested in many 2 to 6 mark questions.

terms.d: A shared pair of electrons between two atoms, usually non-metals; a strong bond.
A group of atoms joined by covalent bonds.
A substance made of small molecules held together by weak intermolecular forces.
Weak forces of attraction between molecules.
A substance with very large molecules made from many small molecules joined together.
A small molecule that joins with many others to form a polymer.
The section of a polymer chain that repeats along the chain, shown in brackets with n.
The reaction in which many unsaturated monomer molecules join to form a polymer with no other product.
A pair of outer-shell electrons that is not shared with another atom.
Two shared pairs of electrons between two atoms.
Three shared pairs of electrons between two atoms.
A diagram that shows the outer electrons of atoms, with dots and crosses for different atoms, including shared pairs.
A formula showing all atoms and bonds in a molecule, with a line for each bond.
The sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in the formula.
A huge network of atoms joined by strong covalent bonds, such as diamond.
The temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas.

worked.ans: Iodine molecules are larger than chlorine molecules (Mr 254 compared with 71), so the intermolecular forces between iodine molecules are stronger. More energy is needed to overcome these forces, so iodine has a much higher melting point and boiling point and is a solid at room temperature, whereas chlorine, with weaker forces, is a gas. In both cases it is the intermolecular forces that are overcome and not the covalent bonds.
worked.q: Chlorine is a gas at room temperature but iodine is a solid. Explain this difference. The relative formula masses are Cl2 = 71 and I2 = 254. [4 marks]
steps: Both are small molecules: the atoms in each molecule are joined by strong covalent bonds, and the molecules are held together by weak intermolecular forces.
Iodine molecules are larger (Mr 254 compared with 71).
Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces.
More energy is needed to overcome them, so iodine has a higher melting and boiling point and is a solid at room temperature.

worked.ans: Poly(ethene) molecules are very large, so the intermolecular forces between them are relatively strong and a lot of energy is needed to overcome them, so it is solid at room temperature. Ethene molecules are small so the intermolecular forces are weak and little energy is needed, so it is a gas.
worked.q: Explain why poly(ethene) is a solid at room temperature but ethene is a gas. [3 marks]
steps: Poly(ethene) has very large molecules, ethene is a small molecule (Mr 28).
Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces.
More energy is needed to overcome the forces in the polymer.

worked.q: A sample of poly(ethene) has a relative formula mass of 56 000. The repeat unit is –CH2–CH2– (Ar of C = 12, H = 1). How many repeat units are in each molecule? [3 marks]
